title: LAN hardware

stations.name: Switch
facts: A switch reads the MAC address in each frame and forwards it only to the device it is meant for. Routers are the ones that use IP addresses.
In a star network every wired device connects through the switch, so if it fails, all the PCs plugged into it are cut off.

questions.q: What does a switch use to send data to the correct device on a LAN?
The switch in a computer room breaks. What happens to the PCs plugged into it?
questions.a: They lose their network connection, because every wired PC connects through the switch

stations.name: UTP cable
facts: Twisting the pairs cancels out electrical interference, including crosstalk between the wires.
The signal in copper UTP weakens over distance, so a run is limited to about 100 m. Fibre optic carries data for kilometres.

questions.q: Why are the copper wires inside UTP cable twisted in pairs?
Why wouldn't you use UTP cable to link two buildings 2 km apart?
questions.a: Each UTP run only works up to about 100 m, so fibre is used for long distances

stations.name: Router
facts: A router joins networks together, such as the school LAN and the internet, and forwards packets using IP addresses.
The printer is on the same LAN, and the switch still links it to the PCs. Websites are on the internet, which can only be reached through the router.

questions.q: What is the main job of a router?
questions.a: To connect different networks and send packets on using IP addresses

questions.q: The router fails, but the switches still work. What can students still do?
questions.a: Print to the class printer, but not load websites

stations.name: Fibre optic cable
facts: Fibre optic cable sends pulses of light along thin strands of glass.
Fibre carries huge amounts of data over thousands of kilometres and isn't affected by electrical interference. It is actually more expensive and harder to install than copper.

questions.q: How does fibre optic cable carry data?
questions.a: As pulses of light through glass

questions.q: Which two reasons best explain why the undersea cables that carry the internet are fibre optic?
questions.a: High bandwidth, and it works over very long distances

stations.name: Wireless access point
facts: A WAP sends and receives radio waves so that wireless devices can join the wired network. It is connected to a switch by cable.
Wi-Fi range is limited and walls weaken the signal, and each WAP can only handle so many devices well. Extra WAPs don't speed up the link from the router to the internet.

questions.q: What does a wireless access point (WAP) do?
questions.a: Lets wireless devices connect to a wired network

questions.q: Why does a large school need lots of WAPs rather than one?
questions.a: Each WAP has a limited range and can only serve so many devices

stations.name: Network interface card
facts: Every NIC has a unique MAC address set by the manufacturer. IP addresses are given out by the network.
Without a wireless NIC the PC cannot use Wi-Fi, so it needs a cable into a switch.

questions.q: What unique address is built into every NIC when it is made?
A desktop PC has a wired NIC but no wireless NIC. How must it connect to the school network?
questions.a: With an Ethernet (UTP) cable to a switch

final.name: Final challenge

questions.q: A student on a laptop opens a website. Put the request's journey in order.
questions.a: The laptop sends the request by Wi-Fi to the wireless access point → The WAP passes it along a UTP cable to the switch → The switch forwards it to the router → The router sends it along fibre optic cable to the internet

final.note: Students should have predicted this on the worksheet before tapping the star.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does.
Giving an advantage with no reason attached.
Repeating the question in the answer.
